ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, shareholders, ultimate beneficial owners and authorized signatories against the New Zealand Sanctions Act 2020, United Nations Security Council consolidated sanctions lists, OFAC Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list, UK OFSI consolidated list, EU consolidated financial sanctions list, Interpol and domestic law enforcement watchlists, and the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit suspicious transaction reporting regime. Enhanced due diligence must include politically exposed persons (PEPs) as defined by the AML/CFT Act 2009, immediate family members and close associates, with a risk-based approach requiring electronic identity verification, source of funds and source of wealth documentation, adverse media screening, and ongoing transaction monitoring. For a high-risk energy commodity trading entity, additional screening against the Financial Action Task Force high-risk and monitored jurisdictions list and the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs designated non-financial business or profession guidelines is required. All screening must be documented and retained for at least five years from the end of the business relationship.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Name Reservation and Company Registration Portal (www.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must be in the English alphabet or Māori with English transliteration; names must be clearly distinguishable from existing registered names, reserved names, and names of overseas companies. The Companies Act 1993 prohibits names that are identical or almost identical to an existing company or registered business name; a four-tier naming hierarchy applies: (1) distinctive element, (2) descriptive element, (3) legal ending or entity type suffix, and (4) any required regulatory consent token. Diacritical marks in Māori are permitted with transliteration guidance but all official registry entries must be searchable in ASCII-compatible form.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Registrar of Companies rejects a proposed name on grounds of indistinguishability, offensiveness, or contravention of a restricted word, the applicant may submit a written request for reconsideration to the New Zealand Companies Office using the formal 'Name Review Request' form. The request must identify the exact registration reference number, restate the proposed name, explain the legitimate business purpose, and provide evidence distinguishing the name from any conflicting registered entity, such as a letter of consent from the existing rights holder where applicable. The Companies Office must respond within 20 working days. If the Registrar maintains the refusal, the applicant may seek judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand under the Judicature Act 1908 and the Companies Act 1993 section 22, filing an originating application within 28 days of the written refusal, citing any procedural error, misapplication of the indistinguishability test, or unreasonable exercise of statutory discretion. During the appeal, the proposed name remains unavailable to third parties only if a pending reservation is extended by the Registrar or an interim injunction is granted.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office or commercial mailbox is permissible for basic directorship and correspondence services but is highly likely to be rejected as proof of registered office and physical commercial substance for a wholesale petroleum and marine fuel trading company. The Companies Act 1993 requires a registered office in New Zealand, but the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) and licensed banks require a physical operating address that can receive inspections, service of process, and commercial records. A company engaged in ISIC 4661 wholesale of crude oil and refined petroleum products must demonstrate substantive business activity, including physical records, bank account management, board meeting locations, and settlement operations in New Zealand. Using a virtual office as the sole commercial footprint will trigger adverse risk ratings, enhanced due diligence, and potential refusal of bank account opening or Goods and Services Tax (GST) registration.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Checklist: (1) confirmation of physical signage at registered office; (2) availability of board meeting minutes and corporate records; (3) access to accounting and bank account records; (4) employment or contractor agreements evidencing New Zealand operational staff; (5) trade and storage contracts or broker agreements; (6) evidence of active banking and settlement channels; (7) tax and GST filings showing actual trading activity. The risk of unannounced physical inspection is moderate-to-high for this sector. The Companies Office, Inland Revenue Department, and Financial Intelligence Unit may conduct compliance visits under the Tax Administration Act 1994 and AML/CFT Act 2009, with heightened audit probability due to the high-risk petroleum wholesale classification and energy sector anti-money-laundering scrutiny.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), particularly sections 12-16 (Incorporation), 30-32 (Constitution), 122-125 (Directors), and 189-190 (Registered Office).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Incorporation of a Company (Form 48) together with the Constitution (if any) and consent to act as director forms
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None - New Zealand law does not impose a minimum paid-up capital requirement for a limited liability company. Shares may be issued for nominal consideration, and there is no requirement for an escrow or blocked account.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
RESOLUTION OF THE FIRST MEETING OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED

Pursuant to the Companies Act 1993 and the Constitution of the Company, the following resolutions were duly passed at the first meeting of the Board of Directors held on [date] at [place].

1. SHARE CAPITAL SUBSCRIPTION: RESOLVED that the initial share capital of the Company be fixed at NZD 1,000 divided into 1,000 ordinary shares of NZD 1.00 each, and that the subscribers to the Memorandum of Incorporation do hereby subscribe for the said shares as set out in the register of members. The directors are hereby authorized to issue additional shares in accordance with the Constitution and the Companies Act 1993, and to determine the terms and conditions of such issuance.

2. BANKING AUTHORIZATION: RESOLVED that the Company be and is hereby authorized to open, operate, and maintain bank accounts with any bank or financial institution in New Zealand or abroad, and to appoint such signatories as the directors may determine. The directors are further authorized to negotiate, execute, and deliver any loan, credit, or guarantee agreements, and to issue standby letters of credit or other financial instruments as may be required for the Company's business, including the use of SWIFT wire transfers.

3. REGISTERED OFFICE: RESOLVED that the registered office of the Company be established at [full address] in New Zealand, and that the Company Secretary be instructed to file the requisite notice of registered office with the New Zealand Companies Office within the statutory timeframe.

4. STATUTORY OFFICERS: RESOLVED that [Name] be appointed as the sole director of the Company, that [Name] be appointed as the Company Secretary, and that [Name] be appointed as the Chief Financial Officer, each to serve until the next annual general meeting or until their successors are duly appointed. The officers are hereby vested with all powers necessary to execute the Company's business and to ensure compliance with all applicable laws.

5. GENERAL COMPLIANCE: RESOLVED that the directors be and are authorized to take all necessary steps to comply with the Companies Act 1993, including the filing of annual returns, maintenance of statutory registers, and engagement of professional advisors as deemed appropriate.

All resolutions were passed unanimously and are recorded in the minutes of this meeting.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office – Online Name Reservation Portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a name availability search on the Companies Office register to ensure the proposed company name is not identical or confusingly similar to an existing entity. Reserve the name via the online portal, which requires submission of the proposed name and payment of a reservation fee (NZD 10). The reservation is valid for 20 business days. Simultaneously, verify that the proposed directors and shareholders meet the eligibility criteria under the Companies Act 1993, including that at least one director resides in New Zealand or is a director of a New Zealand company. Prepare the consent to act forms for each director and shareholder.
required_dossiers: Full legal names, addresses, and dates of birth of all directors and shareholders
Consent to act as director forms (signed)
Proof of identity (passport or national ID) for each director
Residential address verification for each director
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected due to similarity, the applicant may file a formal objection with the Companies Office within 10 working days, providing evidence of distinctiveness or prior use. Alternatively, select an alternative name and resubmit.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Submission of Incorporation Application
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office – Online Incorporation Portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete the Application for Incorporation (Form 48) online, providing the company name, registered office address, director and shareholder details, and the share structure. Attach the signed consent to act forms and any constitution (if adopted). The application must be submitted electronically via the Companies Office website. Ensure that all information is accurate and matches the reserved name. The system will validate the data and calculate the filing fee (NZD 150). Payment is made online via credit card or direct debit. Upon successful submission, the Companies Office will issue an electronic acknowledgement and assign a company number.
required_dossiers: Signed consent to act as director forms
Constitution (if any, signed by all subscribers)
Proof of registered office address (e.g., lease agreement or utility bill)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried due to incomplete information or discrepancies, the Companies Office will issue a notice of deficiency. The applicant must rectify the issues within 15 working days by submitting amended forms or additional documentation. Failure to respond may result in the application being deemed withdrawn, but a fresh application can be submitted.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Certificate of Incorporation and Post-Incorporation Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon approval, the Companies Office will issue a Certificate of Incorporation, which is conclusive evidence of the company's existence. The certificate will be available for download from the online portal. Immediately thereafter, the company must register for tax purposes with the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) by completing the online registration form, obtaining an IRD number, and registering for GST if annual turnover exceeds NZD 60,000. Additionally, the company must open a corporate bank account, which requires the certificate of incorporation, the constitution, and a resolution of the board authorizing the account opening. The company must also appoint a registered office and maintain a share register.
required_dossiers: Board resolution authorizing bank account opening
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD registration is delayed, the company may still operate but must ensure tax obligations are met. For bank account issues, the company may approach alternative banks or provide additional due diligence documents. If the certificate of incorporation contains errors, the company must apply for a correction within 20 working days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) – Energy Markets Branch; Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Given the business scope of wholesale brokerage of marine fuel oil and distillates, the company must obtain a Fuel Industry Participant Registration under the Fuel Industry Act 2020. This registration is mandatory for any entity engaged in the wholesale supply of fuel. The application is submitted online via the MBIE portal, requiring details of the business model, storage arrangements (if any), and compliance with fuel quality standards. If the company intends to store fuel, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) may be required, but for pure brokerage, an exemption is likely. Additionally, the company must register with the New Zealand Customs Service if importing or exporting fuel, and obtain a Customs Client Code. For any physical storage, a Civil Defense fire safety certificate from the local territorial authority is required.
required_dossiers: Fire safety certificate (if storage is involved)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Fuel Industry Participant Registration is refused, the company may appeal to the Fuel Industry Authority within 20 working days, providing additional evidence of compliance. For EIA requirements, if the EPA determines a full assessment is needed, the company must submit an environmental impact report and undergo public consultation. For fire permits, the company can rectify any deficiencies and reapply.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) – Energy Markets Branch

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt (for pure brokerage without physical storage or handling). If storage or handling is added, a Full EIA Report may be required under the Resource Management Act 1991.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable for brokerage-only operations. If storage is introduced, the company must comply with the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality (NES-AQ) and the Resource Management (National Environmental Standards for Sources of Human Drinking Water) Regulations 2007. Wastewater discharge must meet the standards set by the local regional council, typically requiring a discharge permit. VOC emissions from storage tanks must not exceed 0.5% of throughput per annum, and hazardous waste handling must follow the Hazardous Substances (Hazardous Waste) Regulations 2004.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not applicable for pure brokerage. If the company operates a storage facility, it must obtain a Fire Safety Certificate from the local territorial authority under the Building Act 2004, including structural load inspections and compliance with the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) regulations. Additionally, a workplace safety approval under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 is required, including a documented safety management system and emergency response plan.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) of New Zealand; online portal myIR available at myir.ird.govt.nz. Export declarations and customs transactions are lodged with the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window (TSW).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign non-resident entity that will have a New Zealand tax nexus must first register with the New Zealand Companies Office under the Companies Act 1993 if it carries on business in New Zealand, or otherwise establish its legal existence through a foreign certificate of incorporation, constitution, and certificate of good standing. The entity then applies to the IRD for an IRD number via myIR or the standard IRD registration procedure, providing the overseas incorporation documents, registered office or foreign address parameters, directors and ultimate beneficial owners details, expected New Zealand business activity, and tax residency position. The IRD number functions as both the income tax identifier and the GST identifier when GST registration is subsequently obtained. GST registration under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 is mandatory for a person carrying on a taxable activity in New Zealand if total taxable supplies in any 12-month period reach or are expected to reach NZD 60,000. Non-resident suppliers of remote or offshore services to New Zealand consumers may also register through a simplified offshore GST process. Once GST registration is approved, the entity receives its GST number and must lodge GST returns through myIR or IRD-approved digital channels. For marine fuel oil and refined products wholesale brokerage, the entity must also ensure compliance with any statutory licensing from the Environmental Protection Authority for fuel activities and with anti-money laundering registration obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 where applicable.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — a New Zealand resident limited company is taxed at the corporate rate of 28% on worldwide income; a non-resident company is taxed at the same corporate rate on New Zealand-source income only. There is no sub-national income tax, alternatively the territorial scope is nationwide because New Zealand is a unitary tax jurisdiction.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: None in the US check-the-box sense; New Zealand does not provide an entity classification election. A qualifying closely held NZ Ltd may elect Look-Through Company (LTC) status under subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007 if it has five or fewer shareholders and no corporate shareholder, causing income, losses, and credits to flow through to shareholders. Group loss offset elections are available under subpart IC of the Income Tax Act 2007. Hybrid mismatch rules under sections FH 1 to FH 18 of the Income Tax Act 2007 are mandatory and cannot be elected out of.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in a rolling 12-month period for a taxable activity carried on in New Zealand; the same NZD 60,000 threshold applies to non-resident suppliers of remote services where the supplies are made to New Zealand-resident consumers.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not impose a mandatory real-time electronic invoicing clearance system, continuous transaction controls, or digital tax stamping. Electronic invoicing is voluntary and operates through the PEPPOL network under the NZ e-Invoicing initiative. Invoice data is not transmitted to the IRD for each transaction; instead, GST-registered businesses are required to issue tax invoices containing the statutory information in the GST Act and Tax Administration Act 1994 and to retain those records for at least seven years. GST returns are filed electronically through myIR or IRD-compatible accounting software; API-based filing is optional and not a real-time tax clearance requirement.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exports of physical goods are zero-rated under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 where the supplier exports the goods from New Zealand in the course of, or as a condition of, the supply, or where goods are sold to a non-resident customer and are exported from New Zealand within 60 days of the time of supply while the supplier retains satisfactory evidence. For crude oil, marine fuel oil, and refined petroleum products, the relevant categories are direct export through New Zealand Customs, international voyage bunker supplies delivered as ships' stores for an overseas-going vessel, and supplies where the goods are entered for export under the Customs and Excise Act 2018 and are not diverted back to domestic use. Marine fuel delivered to vessels engaged in exclusively coastal New Zealand trade remains standard-rated at 15%. Foreign exchange repatriation is not itself a statutory condition for zero-rating, but the exporter must be able to demonstrate that the supply was made to a non-resident and that the goods moved offshore; bank remittance and SWIFT records are used to support this evidence.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Electronic Export Entry submitted to the New Zealand Customs Service through the Trade Single Window under the Customs and Excise Act 2018
Bill of Lading, Sea Waybill, or Air Waybill evidencing the physical shipment and overseas destination
Bunker Delivery Note or foreign-vessel stores declaration where claiming ships'-stores zero-rating
Commercial invoice and supply contract describing the product, HS classification such as 2710, quantity, Incoterms, consignee, destination, and export value

Bank SWIFT or foreign currency remittance records showing payment from the non-resident buyer; New Zealand does not issue an Inward Remittance Certificate, so underlying bank records are the accepted documentary evidence
Packing list or independent weight and quantity certificate where applicable
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The IRD may reconstruct a supply and assess output GST at 15% if the supporting export document package does not substantiate zero-rating. Shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 include 20% for failure to take reasonable care, 20% for an unacceptable tax position with inadequate evidence, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or arrangements with a dominant purpose of defeating GST. Use-of-money interest accrues from the due date of the relevant return. False or misleading export entries may also trigger prosecution under the Customs and Excise Act 2018, including seizure and forfeiture of goods and recovery of excise-equivalent duty or fuel excise. Where a zero-rated export is later diverted back into New Zealand for domestic consumption, the supply is clawed back as a taxable domestic supply and any input credits previously claimed on the export are reversed. Evidence limited solely to payment receipts is insufficient to defend a zero-rating claim; the customs export entry and transportation documentation are mandatory.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) - Te Putea Matua
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand maintains a fully liberalised currency and capital account regime. The New Zealand dollar is freely convertible under a floating exchange rate system. There is no foreign exchange control act, no central bank approval threshold for trade or financial transactions, and no requirement to surrender export proceeds. Current account and capital account payments may flow freely through registered banks, subject only to standard AML/CFT customer due diligence and cross-border reporting obligations. For a non-resident-owned energy trading entity, equity injections, shareholder loans, dividend distributions, and trade settlement can be effected without Reserve Bank of New Zealand exchange-control approval. The principal legal constraints are the Overseas Investment Act 2005 if a transaction involves sensitive New Zealand land or a special category of significant business assets, and the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 for derivative dealing. Profit remittance is subject to normal corporate tax and non-resident dividend withholding tax under NZ domestic tax law, but no exchange license or compulsory conversion applies. Banking counterparties may impose internal economic sanctions filters and country exposure limits, but these are prudent underwriting constraints, not exchange controls.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: New Zealand operates no statutory export proceeds surrender regime. An exporter may retain, convert, borrow against, or invest foreign currency receipts at commercial discretion. RBNZ collects balance-of-payments survey data for statistical publication; no timeline or mandatory conversion ratio applies. Documentary proof of receipt must be maintained for tax and bank audit trails.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account in NZD and USD
Basic Operational Currency Account with multi-currency sweep
Basic Operational Currency Account with trade finance facility
Capital Escrow Account and Operating Account in USD/NZD

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Low. In New Zealand, entities providing deposit-taking and banking services must be licensed by the RBNZ under the Banking Act. Pure fintech EMIs are not authorised to offer corporate deposit accounts or issue Standby Letters of Credit. They may be registered on the FMA Financial Service Providers Register for certain payment services, but a high-risk petroleum-product wholesale brokerage requires a full-service corporate banking relationship with direct SWIFT membership, correspondent clearing lines, trade finance capacity, and physical AML compliance capability. Offshore digital EMIs lacking an NZ banking licence are legally constrained and will not be accepted as primary treasury rails. Their use is limited to ancillary, pre-funded settlement where the EMI holds a regulated NZ payment service licence. Therefore, this blueprint mandates Tier-1 domestic bank onboarding for all treasury-critical flows.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No statutory requirement exists for directors to appear physically in-branch under New Zealand AML/CFT regulations, but registered banks may impose an enhanced interview mandate for high-risk energy commodity trading structures. Remote video verification is generally accepted for standard entities, subject to notarised passport copies, independent utility bills, and a registered New Zealand address. For a crude oil and refined products wholesale brokerage with non-resident shareholders, banks normally require a physical or high-assurance video interview of all directors and beneficial owners before account opening. Pure consular proxy opening is rare and generally not accepted unless the attorney is validated by a current power of attorney and appears for a separate enhanced identity verification.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership opacity across trust and corporate layers
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete UBO register with official shareholder ledger, trust deed, target-level control chart of every intermediate entity, certified passport copies, proof of address for every person owning or controlling more than 10%, independent legal opinion on control, and a five-year company extract from the New Zealand Companies Office.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions and politically exposed persons (PEP) exposure in global oil trading
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: PEP declaration for all directors and UBOs, sanctions screening outputs from World-Check or LexisNexis with clear hit resolution, refinery and vessel registry documentation, charter-party contracts, country-of-origin certificates, evidence that no UN, EU, UK, or US OFAC SDN sanctions list entry applies, and a counterparty due-diligence file covering all material trading partners.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unclear source of funds for initial capital injection
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Six-month bank statements from the originating corporate account, signed shareholder loan agreements, dividend vouchers, audited financial statements of the parent entity, source-of-wealth declaration from a bank reference, and a sequential source-of-funds waterfall tracer showing movement from original wealth creation to the final NZ escrow deposit.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Trade-based money laundering red flags in physical commodity brokerage
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Evidence of genuine economic activity: executed sale and purchase agreements with INCO terms, commercial invoices, quality and quantity certificates, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, vessel screening certificates, independent petroleum inspector reports, the underlying documentary credit trial balance, and an explanation of commissions or freight margins consistent with prevailing market rates.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound shareholder funds should be routed via a compliant SWIFT MT103 wire from a disclosed corporate account in the shareholder jurisdiction, with transaction narrative referencing 'equity subscription' or 'non-resident shareholder loan'. New Zealand has no exchange-control approval requirement, but banks will require the beneficiary to complete a capital introduction source-of-funds statement, tax residency declaration, and board resolution authorising account opening. The funds must land in a dedicated capital escrow account and are then transferred to the operating account after the Companies Office annual return update and bank AML release. If the equity injection constitutes a sensitive overseas investment under the Overseas Investment Act 2005, an Overseas Investment Office application may be required. Audit confirmation of capital verification must be obtained from the NZ registered bank.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For outbound trade settlements, the principal rails are SWIFT MT103 for open-account payments, SWIFT MT700/MT707 for documentary letters of credit, documentary collections under URC522, and SWIFT MT760 for standby letters of credit or performance guarantees. Payments must clear through the domestic bank's USD correspondent banking network under a strict economic sanctions screening process. Trade documents must be clean, consistent, and matched against the underlying sales contract. For NZD payments, no restriction applies; for foreign currency payments, banks may require an underlying trade invoice and import/export supporting documents to be held on the client file.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forward contracts in NZD/USD and liquid trade currencies, up to 12 months tenor, supported by verifiable underlying trade exposure
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for settlement currency pairs where the underlying currency is not freely deliverable, executed under an approved RBNZ/FMA derivatives licence
Cross-currency interest-rate swaps between NZD and USD for aligning long-dated trade finance and escrow liabilities
Customised currency options with ISDA/CSA documentation, subject to Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 derivative issuer obligations and bank collateral arrangements

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return under Companies Act 1993, sections 209-212
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (NZCO)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No later than the last day of the month following the anniversary of the company's incorporation date, being the notified 'return date' on the New Zealand Companies Register
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file the annual return and pay the prescribed fee is an offence punishable by a fine of up to NZD 10,000 against the company and each director; continued default can lead the Registrar to issue a notice of intention to remove the company from the Register, and after expiry of the notice period the company may be administratively struck off and dissolved with assets vested in the Crown.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Audited financial statements and auditor's report for large companies and FMC reporting entities
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment; Financial Markets Authority for FMC reporting entities if applicable
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a large company with a standard 31 March balance date, financial statements must be filed with NZCO within 5 months after balance date, by no later than 31 August; FMC reporting entities must comply with Financial Markets Conduct Act filing windows
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-filing is an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 carrying fines of up to NZD 10,000 for the company and directors; continuing default may be treated as a Companies Act compliance failure and can trigger Registrar removal action plus FMA enforcement for FMC reporting entities.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Return of Allotment on issue of shares
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the date of allotment of any shares
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to deliver the return of allotment is an offence under section 71 of the Companies Act 1993, with conviction liability of up to NZD 10,000; the Registrar may also require correction and pursue strike-off for persistent non-compliance.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Notice of Change of Registered Office or Address for Service
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 10 working days after the change of registered office or after the company ceases to occupy the registered premises
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-compliance is an offence under the Companies Act 1993 with fines up to NZD 10,000; documents served at the old registered office may be deemed ineffective, and enforcement action may be initiated by the Registrar.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Notice of Change of Directors, Director Resignation, or Director Particulars
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the appointment, resignation, removal, or change of director name or residential address
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to notify constitutes an offence under the Companies Act 1993, with fines up to NZD 10,000; the Registrar may also regard outdated director information as a ground for compliance action and possible Register strike-off.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Company Income Tax Return (IR4) and Financial Summary (IR10)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department of New Zealand (IRD)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 return is due by 7 July following the balance date; terminal tax payment is due by 7 April following the balance date; provisional tax instalments apply during the year for taxable companies
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of NZD 250 applies; late payment penalties accrue at 1% on the day after the due date plus an additional 4% after 7 days and a further 1% monthly continuing penalty; use-of-money interest applies on unpaid tax; persistent non-payment may trigger IRD collection enforcement and director personal liability notices.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: GST return and payment (GST101) for registered taxable activity
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department of New Zealand (IRD)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly filing frequency is assigned by IRD based on turnover and entity profile; returns and payments are due one month after the end of each taxable period, with six-monthly returns covering 1 October-31 March due 7 May and 1 April-30 September due 7 November
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of NZD 250 per GST return; late payment penalties begin at 1% on the day after the due date, increase by 4% after 7 days, and continue at 1% monthly; IRD may set off refunds, garnish bank accounts, and pursue formal debt recovery.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: AML/CFT compliance programme review and supervisor reporting if the entity is a reporting entity under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Respective AML/CFT supervisor, being the Department of Internal Affairs, Financial Markets Authority, or Reserve Bank of New Zealand as allocated
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: The AML/CFT programme, risk assessment, and beneficial ownership CDD records must be reviewed at least annually and updated on material business or control changes; any supervisory annual report must be filed within the deadline given by the supervisor
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-compliance attracts civil liability, regulatory enforcement, public warnings, enforceable undertakings, and monetary penalties that may reach NZD 2 million for bodies corporate in cases of multiple or prolonged breaches; directors may also face disqualification and pecuniary penalties.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996 location approval and environmental compliance certificate, if the entity physically stores or handles fuel oils
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: WorkSafe New Zealand and the relevant regional council having jurisdiction
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Approval and annual compliance certification must remain current; any renewal must be filed before the existing certificate expiry date; immediate notification is required for any incident involving hazardous substance release
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Operating without a current HSNO location certificate is an offence; a body corporate may be fined up to NZD 10,000 for each day the breach continues, and WorkSafe may suspend, restrict, or cancel the approval.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, a company is a large company and must have an independent certified audit if, in each of the two immediately preceding accounting periods, it exceeds at least one of the following quantitative thresholds: (a) total assets exceeding NZD 60 million; (b) total revenue exceeding NZD 30 million; or (c) 50 or more full-time equivalent employees. Compulsory statutory audit also applies to any FMC reporting entity under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 unless an express exemption under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 applies. In addition, the shareholders of a company that is not large may require an audit by a resolution supported by shareholders holding at least 5% of the votes or by at least 100 shareholders, in which case the company must appoint a qualified auditor and prepare audited financial statements for that financial year.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand Equivalents to International Financial Reporting Standards (NZ IFRS) constitute GAAP for large for-profit entities; Tier 2 for-profit entities may apply NZ IFRS with Reduced Disclosure Regime (NZ IFRS RDR); smaller companies may use the XRB's Simple Format Reporting Template and related standards, but tax-basis records do not satisfy generally accepted accounting practice for statutory financial reporting. All statutory accounts must be prepared in accordance with the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and the Companies Act 1993.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand currently does not maintain a public beneficial ownership register in the Companies Office. The Annual Return filed with the New Zealand Companies Office serves as the company's annual confirmation mechanism, stating current shareholders, share classes, paid-up capital, directors, registered office, and address for service. All changes in shareholdings must be documented in the Register of Members immediately upon registration of a transfer; an allotment of new shares must be reported to the Companies Office within 20 working days. Where the company is an AML/CFT reporting entity, beneficial ownership information must be verified and refreshed before providing any new service, and in any case within 30 days after the company becomes aware of a material change in beneficial ownership or control. Non-resident ownership of an NZ limited company is permitted, but if an overseas person acquires a significant interest in sensitive New Zealand business assets, separate consent and reporting obligations under the Overseas Investment Act 2005 must be assessed.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 150 - 600 per annum for registered office and company secretarial agent services in New Zealand
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 12,000 - 45,000 per audit engagement for a medium-sized energy wholesale and petroleum commodity trading entity, depending on consolidated structure, transaction volume, and related-party complexity

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: New Zealand imposes no general statutory tax holidays, free-zone exemptions, or patent box regime. The principal effective rate reliefs are the R&D Tax Incentive (15% refundable credit on eligible R&D expenditure), the imputation credit system that prevents economic double-taxation of distributed corporate profits, and ordinary commercial deductions for brokerage, freight, storage, hedging, and marine fuel wholesaling costs. A commodity wholesale broker is otherwise subject to the 28% corporate tax rate on net taxable income.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: No fixed statutory year limit; New Zealand allows indefinite loss carry-forward for companies satisfying the shareholder continuity and same-business requirements under sections IA 5 and IA 7 of the Income Tax Act 2007.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 — New Zealand Company Income Tax Return, filed electronically through Inland Revenue's myIR Secure Online Portal
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 return and terminal tax are due on 7 October of the following income year, being the 7th day of the 7th month after balance date. Different balance dates shift the due date on the same month-count rule, and tax-agent extension schedules can postpone certain filing deadlines.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total assessable income derived by the New Zealand company from worldwide business, including wholesale marine fuel and crude oil distillate brokerage commissions, trading margins, freight and demurrage recoveries, storage revenues, and incidental energy-trading receipts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a New Zealand tax-resident limited company, report globally sourced income net only of specified permitted deductions. Non-resident-owned structures must separately identify income attributable to New Zealand management, order-taking, or contract negotiation functions. If part of the trading margin is booked in an offshore affiliate, a transfer pricing adjustment must be evaluated before finalising Box 1, and any permanent establishment exposure in New Zealand must be quantified.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Operating costs incurred in producing assessable income: vessel charter and freight costs, storage and terminal fees, insurance, surveyor and inspector fees, clearing and settlement charges, brokerage commissions paid to sub-agents, staff costs, and arm's-length intercompany service or financing charges.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Cross-border payments to associated non-resident enterprises are deductible only to the extent they satisfy the arm's-length and business-like conditions of subpart GC of the Income Tax Act 2007. Interest and royalties paid to non-residents must be brought into the NRWT net before deduction is accepted. Deductions are reduced for any transfer pricing adjustment, non-deductible entertainment, fines, or expenses not connected with taxable income. Do not include the cost of crude oil inventory on a cash basis unless the applicable valuation method is authorised.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 3 — Net Profit / Loss Before Taxes
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The financial accounting profit or loss after matching generally accepted accounting practice (NZ GAAP) income and expenses, before statutory tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the New Zealand entity acts as an energy-trading broker for an offshore principal, the accounting net profit must reflect actual economic functions, assets, and risks borne by the New Zealand company. A paper-only net profit is generally rejected where New Zealand staff negotiate physical deliveries, manage letters of credit, or control counterparty default risk. Show the accounting result before any tax-only adjustments so the IRD can reconcile the IR4 to the audited financial statements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Non-deductible items, transfer pricing corrections, timing differences, foreign exchange hedging adjustments, thin-capitalisation disallowances, prior-year adjustments, and any overstatement or understatement of expenditure.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident controlled companies must prepare a detailed thin-capitalisation schedule if they have cross-border related-party debt; excessive interest deductions are added back under Part FE. Transfer pricing corrections must align with the selected OECD methodology. Foreign exchange gains and losses on oil-trading contracts are included on a realisation basis unless the company validly applies a mark-to-market method. This box is the principal forum for correcting Box 1-Box 3 mismatches.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Assessable profit after all statutory adjustments and, where available, the deductible portion of carried-forward tax losses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For non-resident-owned New Zealand companies, loss carry-forward is denied if shareholder continuity of at least 49% has not been maintained throughout the continuity period. If there has been a change in non-resident equity ownership during the year, compute the fraction of losses available and disclose the continuity calculation. Hedging losses are deductible only where the underlying commodity trading income is assessable and the hedging arrangement is ordinary in the energy wholesale business.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 6 — Tax on Taxable Income at 28%
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The statutory corporate liability calculated by multiplying Box 5 taxable income by the 28% company tax rate.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: This liability is calculated at the entity level regardless of foreign shareholder ownership. No reduction is allowed merely because the ultimate beneficial owner is a non-resident. The New Zealand company must not apply an assumed foreign effective tax rate, treaty credit, or shareholder-level DTA rate to reduce its own box 6 liability except through the specific credit provisions in Box 7.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 7 — Imputation Credits and Tax Credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Credits arising from New Zealand tax withheld on domestic interest/dividends, foreign income tax credits, and imputation credits held in the company's Imputation Credit Account (ICA).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-owned New Zealand company must operate the ICA in the same way as any other resident company and attach imputation credits to dividends actually paid. Imputation credits retained from prior years are reduced if the majority of shares are sold to non-residents unless a continuity exception applies. Foreign tax credits are available only for underlying foreign tax that is legally and economically attributable to the New Zealand company and not to an offshore affiliate.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 8 — Residual Income Tax / Terminal Tax Payable
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The final net tax payable or refundable after applying provisional tax payments, credits, and Box 6 tax, before NRWT and late-payment penalties.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a purely non-resident-owned company, the IR4 still must be filed and any residual tax paid by the statutory due date. A nil return is not accepted merely because no dividend has been declared. The residual tax is a personal liability of the company; directors cannot rely on foreign-parent instructions to delay payment. Refunds are withheld if the company has undisclosed DTA or non-resident tax obligations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 9 — Non-Resident Withholding Tax on Outbound Dividends, Interest, and Royalties
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Declaration of NRWT liabilities arising on amounts paid or credited to non-residents, including dividends, interest, and royalties.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Any dividend declared to a non-resident shareholder must be reported here. Fully imputed dividends attract NRWT at 15%; unimputed dividends attract 30%. Interest and royalties paid to associated or independent non-residents are subject to NRWT at the domestic rate unless a valid DTA claim or Approved Issuer Levy election is held. Supporting Tax Residency Certificates, beneficial ownership declarations, and contracts must be retained for seven years.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 10 — International Dealings Schedule / Cross-Border Related-Party Disclosure
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Supplementary disclosure of related-party transactions, transfer pricing method selected, intercompany financing arrangements, and the amount of cross-border payments for commodities, services, interest, and royalties.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A New Zealand energy-trading company with cross-border related-party transactions above the documentation threshold must prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation and attach a cross-border disclosure schedule. Identify each associated non-resident counterparty, the nature of the marine fuel wholesale transaction, the economic functions performed in New Zealand, the CUP or TNMM benchmark adopted, and any adjustment made. Omission of this disclosure is a separate strict-liability offence and can evidence evasion.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of the IR4 triggers late filing penalties, typically NZ$250 per month for large taxpayers and NZ$50 per month for other taxpayers, subject to statutory caps. Late payment penalties run at 1% immediately, an additional 4% after 7 days, and 1% per month thereafter until the debt clears. Erroneous or fraudulent returns attract civil shortfall penalties of 20%-150% depending on culpability, plus use-of-money interest. Criminal fraud thresholds are reached where the taxpayer knowingly provides false information or omits assessable income; the maximum criminal penalty for tax evasion is a fine of up to NZ$50,000 and imprisonment for up to 5 years.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 15% NRWT for fully imputed dividends; 30% NRWT for unimputed dividends paid by a New Zealand company to a non-resident shareholder.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim a reduced rate under a New Zealand Double Tax Agreement, the non-resident payee must: (1) obtain a current Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from its home tax authority; (2) provide the New Zealand payer with a completed IRD non-resident withholding tax declaration (commonly IR67 or the relevant IRD treaty schedule) before the payment date; (3) certify beneficial ownership and absence of a New Zealand permanent establishment to which the income effectively is connected; (4) where applicable, validate eligibility under the OECD Multilateral Instrument Principal Purpose Test; and (5) retain the TRC, contract, and payment records for at least 7 years. The New Zealand payer must withhold at the domestic statutory rate unless the IRD has accepted or the payer is otherwise statutorily protected in applying the lower treaty rate.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Interest: domestic NRWT is 15%, with a 2% Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) alternative for interest paid to non-residents that satisfies the prescribed conditions, which in practice replaces NRWT on many cross-border interest payments. Royalties: domestic NRWT is 15% on gross royalty payments for use of intellectual property; DTA rates commonly range from 5% to 10% depending on treaty terms, the nature of the royalty, and whether the recipient is a company or individual.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: NZD 10 million in aggregate cross-border associated-party transactions in an income year is the practical threshold triggering the preparation of contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation and a Local File in New Zealand. Groups that are large multinationals for OECD Country-by-Country Reporting purposes, generally those with consolidated global revenue above EUR 750 million, are expected to maintain a Master File in addition to a Local File where material New Zealand related-party transactions exist.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not maintain standalone Economic Substance Regulations in the offshore-registration sense, but substantive economic presence is foundational to New Zealand tax residence, transfer pricing, PE attribution, and DTA protection. The general anti-avoidance rule in section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, the OECD Multilateral Instrument Principal Purpose Test, and New Zealand's application of the Authorised OECD Approach require that profits booked in New Zealand correspond to actual staff, premises, risk control, and strategic decision-making. For a marine fuel and distillate trading entity, Core Income-Generating Activities include negotiation with charterers/sellers, trading and credit-risk management, physical supply chain oversight, and maintenance of settlement accounts; if these CIGAs are carried on in New Zealand, the resulting profit is taxable in New Zealand and cannot be treaty-shifted to a letterbox affiliate.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax evasion / fraudulent suppression of turnover
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately suppressing or misstating wholesale brokerage income from crude oil and refined petroleum products, issuing false invoices through an offshore shell affiliate, recording sham deductible expenses, or using nominee shareholders to conceal the true beneficial owner and taxable income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Section 143B Tax Administration Act 1994 criminalises tax evasion and, on conviction, carries a fine of up to NZ$50,000 and/or imprisonment for up to 5 years. Civil shortfall penalties also apply, including a 150% penalty for evasion or similar culpable conduct and a 100% penalty for an abusive tax position under Part 9 of the Tax Administration Act 1994.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly authorise or participate in tax evasion can be made personally liable for unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest through the piercing of the corporate veil; they face creditor claims under sections 135, 136, and 380 of the Companies Act 1993, criminal imprisonment, disqualification from managing companies, asset restraint orders, and travel bans preventing departure from New Zealand until tax debts are resolved.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML/CFT and sanctions failure in high-risk energy trading
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to conduct customer due diligence and beneficial ownership verification on counterparties using Standby Letters of Credit and SWIFT wire payment rails, failing to detect or report suspicious transactions involving sanctioned crude oil, dark fleet shipping facilitators, or high-risk foreign jurisdictions, and allowing a shell counterparty to use the New Zealand entity as an unregulated payment conduit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 imposes penalties for non-compliance: a body corporate can be fined up to NZ$2 million, while an individual can be fined up to NZ$200,000 and/or imprisoned for up to 2 years per offence. Additional civil asset forfeiture may be pursued under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the limited company can be prosecuted as persons concerned in the management of the reporting entity, exposing them to individual fines, disqualification, and imprisonment. Where a director knowingly permits money laundering through trade-based fraud, personal restitution orders may be made, and cross-border travel or banking restrictions can be imposed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell company / artificial transfer pricing and permanent establishment avoidance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a New Zealand limited company with no real staff, premises, or substantive control over crude oil/refined product trades, while claiming all profit belongs to a non-resident parent or affiliated trader at a non-arm's-length commission, thereby defrauding the New Zealand tax base and artificially avoiding a taxable permanent establishment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Sections BG 1, GA 1, and GB 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 permit the Commissioner to reconstruct the arrangement, disregard the shell, and assess the New Zealand entity as if the CIGAs and associated profit were realised in New Zealand. Transfer pricing adjustments can be made under subpart GC, and the resulting tax shortfall is subject to penalties up to 150% plus use-of-money interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly approve artificial intercompany structures face civil liability under the Companies Act 1993 for reckless trading and fraudulent trading, including personal liability for corporate tax and creditor debts. In egregious cases, criminal sanctions apply under the Tax Administration Act and Crimes Act, with imprisonment, company-director disqualification, and restrictive departure orders requiring full restitution or security before leaving New Zealand.
